column4: ch-007 chunk 1 (Niane: Jenne-Jeno and the western Sudan before Mali)
column5: GHA IV (Niane, 1984): Jenne-Jeno settled from the 3rd century BCE by farmers, herders and ironworkers, copper objects of about 500 CE imply Saharan trade reaching it from Takedda, largest area about 34 hectares, African rice (Oryza glaberrima) cultivated from the 1st century CE; the McIntosh digs show its growth was not caused by Arab trans-Saharan trade, and the Muslim traders later moved to Jenne by about 800. Confirms Module 1 lesson 4 (occupation from about 250 BCE); adds the rice and copper details and the 34 hectare figure (Reader gives 33).

column4: ch-007 chunk 1 (Niane: fall of Koumbi, Takrur, Soso)
column5: GHA IV states that Koumbi Saleh fell to the Almoravids in 1076 and calls the following period one for which written sources are few (al-Bakri 1068 to al-Idrisi 1154); it treats the Almoravid capture as fact, in contrast to the Conrad and Fisher doubts the course tags [CONTESTED]. Also: Takrur on the Senegal rose after the eleventh century; Timbuktu founded about 1100 by Tuareg (Magcharen), quoting al-Sa'di; the Soso under Sumaguru Kante (1200-35) opposed Muslim rule, and Mali's chronology rests on Ibn Khaldun's reign lengths and is relative only. Show GHA's confident 1076 beside the sceptics, as a 1984 volume.

column4: ch-007 chunk 2 (Niane: Sundiata, Kirina and the oral schools)
column5: GHA IV: Mali's origin story rests on oral 'schools' of griots (Keyla near Kangaba, Kita, Niagassola, Fadama), whose Sundiata accounts agree on essentials; the Keita claimed descent from Bilal, the Prophet's muezzin, a common Sudanic adoption of Muslim ancestors; Sumaguru Kante's Soso defeated at Kirina, 1220 to 1235 for the war, with Ibn Khaldun and Ibn Battuta as the only Arab writers naming Sundiata ('Mari-Diata', converted by Mudrik, reign twenty years) and no Arab author mentioning Kirina. Niane writes that without Ibn Battuta and Ibn Khaldun historians might have treated Sundiata as a legend. Confirms the course's use of the Sundiata epic as an oral source and its dates as approximate; use for Module 1 lesson 2 and Module 4 lesson 1. A real, citable GHA reference.

column4: ch-007 chunk 3 (Niani, the 'constitution', Mali's kings)
column5: GHA IV: tradition gives Sundiata a constituent assembly at Kurukan Fuga (sixteen noble clans, five marabout clans, four craft castes, joking relationships, fratrilineal succession) which Niane says mixes early and much later material; Mali was a federation of provinces whose rulers kept titles, with two military commands (Sankar Zuma in the south, Faran Sura in the north, from al-Sa'di via al-Umari); the capital Niani on the Sankarani has been excavated since 1968 by a Guinean-Polish team (earth-brick houses in dispersed hamlets, an Arab quarter, a mosque with mihrab, a circular wall around the royal villa), matching al-Umari's description of clay houses without a city wall; Mali's king list is from Ibn Khaldun with Musa I reigning about 1307 to 1332 or 1337 (text and figure disagree) and the pilgrimage dated 1325. Adds archaeology of Niani and a second source for the Sa'di administration line (Module 4 lesson 1); the 'constitution' is [TRADITIONAL DATE] and should not be dated to 1235 as fact.

column4: ch-007 chunk 4 (Niane on Mansa Musa, al-Tuedjin, the voyage)
column5: GHA IV: Musa I reigned 1307 to 1332 (Delafosse's correction of Ibn Khaldun's 25 years) and made the pilgrimage in 1325; the retinue figures (60,000 porters, 500 slaves with gold staffs of over 500 mithqals, 80 loads of gold dust) are quoted from Delafosse and Niane says Arab figures are 'probably exaggerated'; the architect Ishak al-Tuedjin (as-Sahili) built the great mosque at Gao, the Djinguereber and palace at Timbuktu, and an audience chamber at Niani for 12,000 mithqals; al-Umari's story of the predecessor's 200 ships then 2,000 ships is reported with the first fleet at 200 (the young readers' book says 400), and Niane calls the Sertima Atlantic theory 'enticing, but unproved'; oral tradition dislikes Musa for wasting the treasury. Supports the course on Musa, the architect and the unproven voyage, and gives a published GHA reference where Diop doubts the Gao mosque; the pilgrimage year 1325 matches the course's 1324 to 25.

column4: ch-007 chunk 5 (Niane's Mali population and administration)
column5: GHA IV estimates Mali's population at 40 to 50 million and Niani at 'at least 100,000' in the 14th century (the latter from a Leo Africanus count of 6,000 hearths at 10 per household giving 60,000), from sources that say only that the country was dense; Reader puts the whole of sub-Saharan Africa at about 47 million in 1500 by back-projection, so the two cannot both stand. Neither is a count. Show both as [THIN EVIDENCE] in Module 4 lesson 2 and Module 8, and say a 1984 volume's figure rests on chronicle phrases such as 400 towns and 7,077 villages. Administration: a confederation of twelve provinces under farin governors, a santigui treasurer, a griot spokesman (Kouyate clan), cavalry of quiver-bearers, and an army of 'about 100,000' as an order of magnitude only; Tellem and Dogon are placed in the Niger Bend with pottery links to Niani.

column4: ch-008 (Ly-Tall, decline of Mali)
column5: After Mansa Musa II (about 1387) Mali's decline: succession struggles between Sundiata's senior line and the junior line from Mande Bory, two mansas assassinated in three years; Tuareg took Timbuktu about 1433 and most Sahel towns (Walata, Nema, possibly Gao) before Sunni Ali; trade shifted to Gambia markets (Sutuco, Jagrancura) as Portuguese arrived after Ceuta 1415. Arab sources thin after Ibn Khaldun (to 1393-4) until Leo Africanus; Portuguese accounts (Ca da Mosto 1455, Gomes 1456, Pacheco Pereira 1505-6, Fernandes 1506-7, Alvares d'Almada 1594) fill the gap. Add to Module 4 as the decline story: Mali did not simply 'fall' to Songhai.

column4: ch-008 (horses and slaves)
column5: Ly-Tall says Portuguese exchanged horses for slaves, 'to begin with, one horse for eight slaves, but soon it was one for fifteen' (Gambia, 15th-16th century), giving another figure beside Reader's ten to fifteen in the 1450s; ratios are a rough tradition of the trade, not a fixed price. Keep Reader's range and add GHA's as agreement that the rate rose over time. Module 8.

column4: ch-008 (western Mandingo society)
column5: Western Mali: matrilineal succession (nephew chosen), red-water ordeal for sorcery that produced captives, Islam a veneer among chiefs, Kaabu kept traditional religion in the 15th century, and Fulani under Tengella and Koly (Denianke) moved in 1481-1514 until Songhai's Askiya Muhammad's brother killed Tengella 1511-12 per Ta'rikh al-Sudan (1512-13 per al-Fattash). Dates are chronicle dates, flag [PROBABLE]; Koly's descent from Sundiata is called a legend by the chapter. Module 4.

column4: ch-008 end (Ly-Tall, Mali after 1500)
column5: Mali remained as a Gambia-and-Casamance power to the 1590s: Mansa Mahmud II's letter to Portugal (1481-95 embassies) claimed rivalry only with Yemen, Baghdad, Cairo and Takrur sultans (the chapter notes he probably exaggerated); the last bid on Jenne was in 1599 by Mansa Mahmud IV, beaten by the Moroccans after the Kala Chaa changed sides; the empire then crumbled into small states and the Bambara kingdoms of Segu and Kaarta rose in the 1600s; Kaabu stayed the bastion of traditional religion to the 19th century; Mandingo drifted south along kola routes. Module 4: shows Mali declined over 200 years, not at one blow. [PROBABLE] for chronicle dates.

column4: ch-009 chunk 1 (Cissoko, Gao before Sunni Ali)
column5: Songhai before Sunni Ali (1464-92) is thinly known: GHA says Arab sources raise more questions than they answer and oral tradition gives a poor picture; Gao was the capital of a Dia/Za dynasty in the 12th century, the Dia Kossoi converted to Islam in 1019 per the chronicles (the people did not follow), the Gao-Sane stelae (dated 1103 and 1140 in the plates) bear names not in the chronicles and may have been imported; Mandingo conquest dated about 1275 or more likely 1285-1300 (Monteil) not Delafosse's 1324-5; Musa built a mosque at Gao in 1324-5; Mali's grip ended by the late 14th century. Module 4: cite the 1019 conversion and the stelae as chronicle-plus-archaeology, with dates [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-009 chunk 2 (Sunni Ali and Askiya Muhammad)
column5: Sunni Ali reigned 1464-92; took Timbuktu 1468 and Jenne, beat the Mossi king Nasere near Jenne in 1483, died by accident 1492; GHA says he has been rehabilitated: the Timbuktu ulama's picture of a cruel tyrant comes from scholars writing two centuries later (the chronicles of the 1650s) and from a political and religious quarrel, so call it hostile source bias [CONTESTED]. Askiya Muhammad (Ture/Sylla, Soninke) seized power after a civil war in 1492-3, made the pilgrimage 1496-7 with 800 horsemen and about 300,000 dinars, took the title caliph of the Sudan; took Agadez, Katsina and Kano (the chapter says); was overthrown by his sons in 1528; reign list to Muhammad Gao 1592. Module 4.

column4: ch-009 chunk 2 (Songhai collapse)
column5: Songhai fell not only to Moroccan guns but to civil war: the 1586-8 succession struggle (al-Sadduk's revolt against Ishaq II) left the west disillusioned and some princes joined the Moroccans in 1591; the Teghazza salt-mine dispute with the Saadi sultans ran from Ishaq I (1539-49) to the Moroccan seizure under Muhammad III (1583-6); Songhai's centralised, absolute monarchy (hi koi, fari mondzo, kadis) differed from Ghana/Mali federations. Module 4; avoid 'fell because of guns alone'.

column4: ch-009 chunk 3 (Songhai state and economy)
column5: Songhai administration: two big provinces (Kurmina west, Dendi south-east), the Kurmina fari ranked second with an army of almost 4,000, towns such as Timbuktu, Jenne, Walata ran by koi and a kadi; vassals (Kano, Katsina, Agadez, Kel Antessar) ruled indirectly; Mali paid tribute only intermittently. Army: standing force about 4,000 plus 300 sunna guards; at Tondibi 1591 'nearly 30,000 infantry and 10,000 horsemen' - the chapter says true size is not known, so show as an unsourced chronicle number [THIN EVIDENCE]; horse worth about ten captives in the 16th century; Niger flotilla about 2,000 canoes. Economy: salt blocks of 25-30 kg, gold from Bambuk, Bure, Bitu in Asante, imports of cloth from Venice, Florence, Genoa; trade 'did not revolutionize' social structure; slave estates worked by communities under overseers (fanfa). Module 4 and, for slave estates, Module 8.

column4: ch-009 chunk 3 (Timbuktu kadis)
column5: The kadi family of Mahmud ben Umar al-Aqit held the Timbuktu judgeship and Sankore imamate through the 16th century (1498-1548 for Mahmud); Maliki law was taught at 'Sudanese universities' and kadis could not be appealed. Supports course material on Timbuktu's scholars; a family monopoly, not a meritocracy. Module 4.

column4: ch-009 chunk 4 (Timbuktu population and learning)
column5: Cissoko says Timbuktu 'may have had some 80,000' under Askiya Dawud, calls it 'very approximate', prefers it to Mauny's 25,000; Jenne 30,000-40,000; Gao 'nearly 100,000' from a late-16th-century census of 7,626 houses. Show as a range 25,000-80,000 for Timbuktu [THIN EVIDENCE] and not a single figure. Timbuktu 'university' was not an organised institution but independent schools (Sankore etc.); about 180 Koranic schools, 'thousands of students' (no count); three mosques Jingereber, Sidi Yahya, Sankore (the last two built in the first half of the 15th century); Ahmad Baba 1566-1627, Mahmud Kati/Akit 1463-1548 for the kadi. Scientific and mathematical learning 'very rudimentary'; 'virtually nothing' of the written output survives. Module 4.

column4: ch-009 chunk 4 (Islam in Songhai)
column5: Islam in Songhai was urban and elite: the peasants stayed with traditional religion (Harke Dikko river god, Dongo thunder god, the sonianke healers), the cult of the dead continued; Askiya Muhammad wrote to al-Maghili (Tuat) and consulted al-Suyuti (Cairo); the Sudanese intellectual culture 'remained marginal to society and collapsed with the cities which gave rise to it'. Songhai society: nobility, free, guild members, slaves; rural slave rents 'never crushing' is Cissoko's inference from the chronicles, treat as [CONTESTED] beside the course's slavery material. Module 4 and Module 8.

column4: ch-009 chunk 4 (Jenne)
column5: Jenne: an island in the inner delta, 30,000-40,000 people, citing Keech and McIntosh 1980 (excavations) for the revision; links with GHA IV Mali chapter: Jenne-Jeno was inhabited from about the 3rd century BCE. Module 1 and 4 should say Jenne (the later town) replaced Jenne-Jeno by about the 13th century; the chapter does not date that move itself.

column4: ch-012 chunk 1 (Adamu, Hausa origins and Kano)
column5: Hausa origins are open: four theories (Baghdad legend rejected; Saharan; Lake Chad west shore per Sutton; autochthonous per Adamu), none proved; 'Hausa' was a language name before it was an ethnonym (16th-17th century in writing); the Bayajida legend is read as dynastic change, not an Arab immigration, and the chapter says plainly the Coptic, Nubian or Berber origins belong to the defunct Hamitic myth. Kano Chronicle was composed about 1890 from older records; Palmer's date of 999 for Bagauda is 'plainly arbitrary and very approximate'; Gijimasu (1095-1134) founded the present city, Yaji 1349-85 with Wangara (Dioula) Muslims; Rumfa 1463-99. Module 4 or the Hausa material in Module 5: give dates as chronicle dates [TRADITIONAL DATE].

column4: ch-012 chunk 2 (Hausa city-states)
column5: Katsina under Muhammad Korau (1445-95) built a walled birni at a trade crossing with an iron mine; Usman's work disproves a Wangara founding; Abdullahi Smith shows Palmer's Katsina dates are over 100 years too early (eclipse reference). Zazzau: Smith (two towns Turunku and Kufena merged about 1500) against Last's rival theory (Kangoma kingdom of 1200, Hausa rule only from 1641), which the chapter calls conjecture; Queen Amina was a princess and general, never on any king list, dated early 16th century by the editors (Kano Chronicle puts her in 1421-38) [CONTESTED]. Rano's early independence is doubtful (Last): Zamnagaba should replace it among the seven. Kebbi's Kanta broke from Songhai in 1516, died 1556; Hausa states then stopped tribute. Module 4/5: say Hausa city-state dates are chronicle dates, revised downward.

column4: ch-012 chunk 3 (Songhai conquest of Hausaland)
column5: The old belief that Askiya Muhammad conquered Hausaland about 1500-1515 rests only on Leo Africanus; Fisher (1978), cited by Adamu, shows neither the Hausa chronicles nor the Timbuktu chronicles mention it (the Timbuktu ones note only a small expedition to Katsina in 1514), so 'it now appears more than likely that the Songhay conquest of Hausaland never took place'. This contradicts GHA IV's own Cissoko chapter (Askiya took Kano and Katsina), a conflict inside the series that the course should show. Module 4: say Songhai did not govern Hausaland; Kebbi under Kanta broke from Songhai in 1516. [CONTESTED].

column4: ch-012 chunk 3 (Bornu, Jukun, Nupe, Bauchi)
column5: Bornu and Hausa: Kano and Katsina paid tribute to Bornu after about 1425 (Katsina 100 slaves a year) but how far Bornu ruled Hausaland needs research (M. G. Smith: only Biram and Kano at first); the Kanuri sent titles (galadima, chiroma, kaigama). Jukun (Kwararafa, 'salt people') had two centres, Benue and Gongola, with no written or drum history, so their state of 1200-1600 is known from outside sources; Nupe's Tsoede early 16th century but date 'quite uncertain' and he personifies state formation; Bauchi peoples were slave-raided from Kano and Zazzau. Module 4/5 Hausa-neighbours material; [THIN EVIDENCE] on Jukun.

column4: ch-012 chunk 4 (Islam in Hausaland)
column5: Islam reached Hausaland before the Kano Chronicle's Wangara mission of 1349-85: via Kanem-Bornu (eleventh century), via Gobir/Marandet and Arabic loanwords through Kanuri; Muslim names in Kano before Yaji; the Wangarawa Chronicle (1650-1) puts Wangara and al-Maghili together under Rumfa but GHA says it conflates events over a century apart, so prefer the fourteenth-century date for the Wangara but treat all dates as uncertain [CONTESTED]. Islam in Hausaland stayed elite and urban until the 15th century; al-Maghili's 1491-2 visit and essay on princes for Rumfa; Rumfa also accused of 'dishonest ways' by the Hausa Chronicle; Fulani arrived in Yakubu's time (1452-63) from Mali bringing books; Tuareg took Agadez and set up the sultanate there in 1495. Module 4/5: Islam was slow and uneven, not one conversion event.

column4: ch-012 chunk 5 (Hausa state and economy)
column5: Hausa states: small farming hamlets under a maigari, villages, then walled birane under a sarki; sarki absolute in theory with a council of nine (Kano and Gobir) copied from Kanem-Bornu's twelve; Rumfa first used slaves and eunuchs in office (weakening old lineages); a galadima said to have founded 21 towns each of 1,000 slaves under Abdullahi Burja (1438-52), a chronicle figure. Economy: iron ore at Dala hill drew settlement to Kano; every Hausa was primarily a farmer; royal, family and individual fields; textile (cotton, indigo), leather, iron (marmara furnaces), guilds, markets with brokers (dillali); no Hausa ajami manuscript before 1600 is known. Module 4/5: Hausa wealth rested on farming and slave estates as well as trade.

column4: ch-012 chunk 6 (Hausa trade)
column5: Hausa trade: currency was cotton bands, salt and slaves; cowries mentioned at Katsina in a 16th-century source, earlier than the 18th century once assumed; Wangara role in Hausa long-distance trade 'somewhat exaggerated' (North Africans, Tuareg, Kanuri took part); Kano and Katsina were termini of the trans-Saharan route; slaves came from the south, used as currency, servants, soldiers and farm labour, bayi (captured or bought) vs cucenawa (second generation, nearer serfdom); Hausa vocabulary has over fifty words for salt; after Songhai fell (1591) Katsina became the main Saharan terminus. Module 4/5 and Module 8 on slavery inside Africa.

column4: ch-019 chunk 1 (Matveiev, Swahili origins and trade)
column5: Matveiev (1984) builds the Swahili community on Bantu-speaking people with Arab, Persian and Indian additions, with an elite and slaves in the 12th century, and calls 12th-15th century the heyday before the Portuguese; towns were mostly huts with some stone buildings; Manda (Lamu archipelago) led in the 9th-12th centuries, then Kilwa; Kilwa Chronicle used for the Shirazi dynasty and the mid-13th-century war with Shanga, with Abu'l-Mawahib in the early 14th century; Kilwa imported Chinese Sung porcelain from the mid-12th century, gold the chief export; Mogadishu had its own links with Egypt (makdasht cloth). The chapter has the Swahili as a Bantu-based mix rather than 'Arab colonies'. Module 6.

column4: ch-019 chunk 2 (Swahili trade, Islam, architecture)
column5: Matveiev: Islam on the Swahili coast was voluntary, not imposed; islands first (10th century report by al-Masudi), coast itself in the 13th century, with Muslim and African titles (sultan, mfalme) side by side; Ibn Battuta 1331 finds Mogadishu deeply Islamised; Kiswahili written in Arabic script devised by Swahili themselves (Misiugin, 10th-13th century). Chinese ships did not sail beyond Sumatra and Java until Zheng He's voyages of 1417-19 and 1421-2 (Velgus), so the Chinese porcelain at Kilwa arrived through Indian Ocean traders. Kilwa copper and silver coins from the Shirazi dynasty (about the late 12th century per Chittick), Mogadishu coin dated 1322; Kilwa Island purchased for a length of cloth in the chronicle. Stone building from the 12th century with coral blocks, Husuni Kubwa (al-Hasan ibn Sulayman II, 1310-33), Great Mosque rebuilt under Sulayman (1412-42). The chapter notes the Freeman-Grenville view that the stone houses copy mud-wall African plans, against Kirkman and Chittick's Arab-Persian spur; give both [CONTESTED]. Module 6.

column4: ch-019 chunk 3 (who built the Swahili towns)
column5: Matveiev names the 'Persian/Arab founders' reading as a 19th-century theory (Strandes) resting on Hegelian ideas that survives in Gray, Mathew, Oliver, Freeman-Grenville and Kirkman, and sets against it the view (Chittick, Misiugin, Ki-Zerbo, Diop) that the ruling dynasties were local African: Pate's mfalme title passed by 'ndugu' generation rule through women of the Wapate clan, and the Kilwa Chronicle shows the same rule broken. Shirazi legends are read as status claims, like Solomon in Ethiopia, Sayf Dhu Yazan at Kanem, a Prophet link for the Keita; Sutton and Garlake call Swahili stone building 'non-creative', which Matveiev disputes. The Persian-origin line is therefore a legend about prestige, not settled history; the course should state Swahili as an African Bantu-based coastal culture in contact with Arab and Persian traders and teachers [CONTESTED]. Module 6.

column4: ch-019 chunk 3 (decline and the economy's weakness)
column5: Matveiev argues Swahili wealth rested on trade not on growth of productive forces (few iron tools in excavations, goods made for export) and that the main cause of decline was Portuguese naval war, with Zimba raids and a rainfall decrease as lesser factors; Kilwa's fort gateway and Songo Mnara mosque plates as sources. This is Matveiev's view, so place it as a position [CONTESTED], with Reader's and Rodney's Indian Ocean material. Module 6.

column4: ch-022 chunk 1 (Fagan, Zambezi-Limpopo 1100-1500)
column5: Fagan (1984) says all serious scholars now see Great Zimbabwe as an essentially African development, but the ultimate causes of the political and economic organisation behind it 'remain cloaked in mystery'; Leopard's Kopje tradition (11th-12th century, probable immigrants, speculation as to origin), first gold workings south of the Zambezi about the 12th century, terraced Mapela Hill with elite huts, Mapungubwe summit rulers in the 15th century (GHA dates; later excavation moved Mapungubwe earlier, which this volume does not say), Kalomo culture (cattle, imported east-coast glass beads, cowries) and the Gumanye settlement at Great Zimbabwe from about the 10th-11th century (date uncertain). Whether Mapungubwe ruled by a minority group and its link to Great Zimbabwe 'still a matter for debate'. Module 7: keep dates as GHA's with note that Mapungubwe is likely older [unverified, from outside this volume].

column4: ch-022 chunk 2 (how Great Zimbabwe arose)
column5: Fagan sets out two theories of the state's origin: Abraham's religious hypothesis (Shona immigrants, Mwari cult, shrine Dzimba dzemabwe, unpublished oral tradition) and the trade hypothesis (imports of Syrian glass, Persian faience and Chinese celadon in the 14th century; a Kilwa coin of al-Hasan b. Sulayman about 1320-33 found at Great Zimbabwe), and rejects a single cause: both mattered with farming and population growth. Architecture: Acropolis stone walls from the 13th century, Great Enclosure built progressively over the following century (wall average 7.3 m high, 5.5 m thick, 52 m of chevron decoration); conical tower of unknown purpose; granite exfoliation gave blocks of 50-100 cm; 'nothing alien to African practice' except the tower; Arab influence 'almost impossible to detect'; about 150 ruins in the granite country; Zimbabwe-style ruins dated 14th-16th centuries. Module 7: GHA says that the walls were 13th-14th century; ties to Kilwa gold via Sofala.

column4: ch-022 chunk 3 (Ingombe Ilede, decline of Great Zimbabwe)
column5: Ingombe Ilede: 11 rich burials about 1400 (conus shell, gold, copper wire tools, imported glass beads, copper cruciform ingots, Chedzugwe pottery), 31 poor burials alongside, showing stratification; salt of the Lusitu may explain its middleman role (Fagan calls this 'purely hypothetical'); link to Fernandes's 1514 'Mobara' widely accepted. Great Zimbabwe fell into disuse towards the end of the 15th century, power moved south and west under the Rozwi, the first Mwene Mutapa Mutota with son Mutope northwards, southern part broke away about 1490 under Changamire; Fagan's cause: farm land and grazing exhausted around a large non-farming centre (shifting cultivation), a hypothesis stated with 'may' and 'seems very likely'. Mwene Mutapa means 'master pillager' or 'lord of metals' (disputed). Module 7: show decline as one explanation [CONTESTED], not as settled fact.

column4: ch-023 chunk 1 (Vansina, Equatorial Africa and Angola sources and society)
column5: Vansina says the evidence for 1100-1500 is thin: the first extant manuscript on Kongo is 1492, written sources only deal with Kongo, oral traditions first recorded in 1624 and by Dapper and Cavazzi 1641-67, so everything before 1500 'merely consists of hypotheses'; he accepts that Bantu migrations ended before 1000 and says Greenberg's Benue-Cross origin and Oliver/Guthrie's Shaba origin remain disputed (Module 1 and 6: Bantu expansion is contested). States grew from lineage chiefs and 'lords of the land' who absorbed other lineages, with surplus, beer or wine tribute and domestic slaves as extra labour; matrilineal belt; cross-shaped copper ingots as money about 1000, the nzimbu unit in Kongo in 1483, raffia cloth squares about 1500. Module 6; mark Kongo origins [THIN EVIDENCE].

column4: ch-023 chunk 2 (forest, savannahs, Luba beginnings)
column5: Vansina: the equatorial forest was a filter, not a barrier (coastal and river routes; double iron bells of tonal-language makers crossed it before 1450; bwami associations of the Lega may be the source of Great Lakes chiefship ideas). Some societies chose not to form states (Gbaya, Sara-lineage systems), so 'state' was a choice, not an inevitable stage. Sanga excavations and cross-shaped copper ingots from the ninth to twelfth centuries link the Lualaba to the Zambezi, with a probable link to Indian Ocean trade; the Luba state 'emerged before 1500' by a vague estimate and its origin myth (Kongolo) is debated: some think the Luba and Lunda traditions are 19th-century reflections, de Heusch accepts them as myths made when the empires were born; the analysis 'still has to be undertaken'. One Lunda state existed before 1450 (Miller). Module 6: Luba/Lunda dating [THIN EVIDENCE].

column4: ch-023 chunk 3 (Kongo before 1500)
column5: Kongo and Loango formed 'between the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries' by slow amalgamation (Vansina probable, not proved; first states north of Malebo 'perhaps even around 1000'); only excavation of Mbanza Kongo can date it. Founder Lukeni Nimi (Nimi a Lukeni) crossed from Bungu and 'shared' power with Mbanza Kongo's lord (the kabunga priest kept ritual role). Six core provinces about 1483 (Soyo, Mbamba, Nsundi, Mpangu, Mbata, Mpemba), governors nominated by the king (Mbata elected, Soyo hereditary), tribute in nzimbu shells, raffia squares, ivory, skins; the Pigafetta-Lopes description (1591) gives an army of 400,000 for Mbamba, which the chapter says is surely exaggerated; claims to sovereignty over Loango, Teke and Suku about 1530 are 'probably an exaggeration'. Module 6 Kongo: use a flat sentence on founders and dates as [TRADITIONAL DATE].

column4: ch-023 chunk 3 (Lunda, Ovimbundu, southern Angola)
column5: Lunda 'perpetual kingship' (successor takes the predecessor's name and relations) practised before 1500 in the upper Kwango region, a tool for empire only after 1500; Lozi state partly prompted by Lunda, date unknown; Ovimbundu states (first perhaps Kulembe, shortly after 1500) with kilombo military initiation; Feti radiocarbon dates 710+-100 and 1250+-65; Herero and Ambo came from the Zambezi with cattle, Herero got sheep from the Khoi. Module 6 or 7: central and south-western Africa side notes; flag Luba-Lunda state size before 1800 as disputed (Wilson against Yoder, Reefe) [CONTESTED].

column4: ch-023 chunk 4 (Kongo institutions, conclusions)
column5: Kongo kings were chosen by a college of nine or twelve electors (kabunga veto, Mbata governor a member), nominally limited power, king called nzambi mpungu 'superior spirit', incest with a sister marks his separation (a source-reported ritual); capital Mbanza Kongo (Banza) with stone walls was a commercial hub, 'not yet excavated thoroughly'; three orders: aristocracy, free, slaves; slave trade 'limited before 1483' if existing. Vansina's conclusion: the forest was misjudged (not a barrier), early states grew where forest and savannah met, and the sources 'have not yet all been drawn upon'. Module 6: shows Kongo statehood before 1483 was home-grown, with the sources thin.

column4: ch-018 chunk 1 (Tamrat, Horn 13th century)
column5: Tamrat: by 1270 the Zagwe gave way to the Solomonid dynasty; other states existed (Falasha, Gojjam, Damot on the Shoa plateau; Muslim principalities Ifat, Dawaro, Adal, Fetegar, Hadya, Bali, Shoa) about which 'almost nothing is known'; linguistics: the idea that Ethio-Semitic came with South Arabian immigrants after 700 BCE 'no longer seems plausible' (North and South separated at least three centuries before Aksum); Geez literary since the 4th century; the word 'Somali' first appears in an Ethiopian hymn of the early 15th century. Trade shifted from Dahlak to the Zeila route by the mid-13th century, a key factor in Ifat's rise and the southward shift of Ethiopia's centre; Yikunno-Amlak's 'restoration' claim obscures practical reasons. Ibn Battuta's Zeila and Mogadishu (cloth, sultan, qadis, Shafii rite). Module 2: Ethiopia after Aksum and Horn gaps; Somali coast material fills the 'Somalia/Horn' gap.

column4: ch-018 chunk 2 (Yikunno-Amlak and Amde-Siyon)
column5: Yikunno-Amlak took power in 1270 chiefly on trade, military and alliance strength (Muslim horsemen in his army, per his letter to Baybars), not on the 'restored Solomonic' claim, which the chapter calls legitimising polemic. The 'mountain of the kings' (Mount Geshen) confined male relatives to prevent succession wars; Amde-Siyon (1314-44) conquered Damot, Hadya, Gojjam and the Falasha area (about 1316-17), crushed Ifat in 1332 and made Ifat, Dawaro, Sharkha and Bali tributaries; al-Umari's '99 kings under him' is 'almost certainly fanciful'; the empire was 'not a unitary state' but a loose confederation held by garrisons and a court always on campaign. Christians and Muslims in Shoa had lived with mutual toleration under the traditional-religion king of Damot before this. Module 2: replace the Solomonic-genealogy framing with economics and conquest; flag Kebra Nagast as legitimising text (already done).

column4: ch-018 chunk 3 (mobile court, Church, revenue)
column5: Tamrat: Solomonid Ethiopia was governed from a mobile court with 'no large urban areas'; indirect rule; revenue from tribute, fiefs (land grants for service), and control of trade (habasha slaves, ivory, gold, caravans of the emperors' own agents); Church revival from the monastic school of Iyesus-Mo'a on Lake Hayk, Tekle-Haymanot (about 1215-1313) and Ewostatewos, bishops sent from Egypt's Alexandria patriarchate; monasteries were the only schools; Church tied to the empire and 'never gained the heart and soul of the conquered peoples'. Lalibela plates are in the chapter, but the chapter text does not date Lalibela's churches itself in this chunk. Module 2: Ethiopian monastic/Church material; avoid claiming Lalibela was built in one reign unless a source here says so.

column4: ch-018 chunk 4 (Ethiopia and Egypt, decline)
column5: Ethiopia-Mamluk relations: Amde-Siyon's son Seyfe-Ar'ad (1344-70) and Dawit (1380-1412) pressed on Egypt over Copts; Yishak (1413-30) tried an alliance with Europe, his 1427-9 delegation was caught and its leader hanged in Cairo; Zera-Yakob (1434-68) sent a mission to Rome and Naples in 1450, held an Egyptian envoy four years, and was cut off from new bishops 1458-1480; Ethiopian communities stood in Jerusalem, Cyprus, Rome, Venice (the Prester John identification began here). Zera-Yakob founded Debre-Birhan, reconciled the Ewostatewos monks, and suppressed traditional religion; after Baeda-Maryam (1468-78) the succession split weakened the empire before Imam Ahmad's jihad (about 1527-43). Module 2: Ethiopia 1270-1500 as a Christian highland empire dependent on Egypt's patriarchate and on Red Sea trade, not isolated.

column4: ch-025 chunk 1 (Esoavelomandroso, Madagascar)
column5: Madagascar 12th-16th centuries: the GHA says the essential peoples were present by the end of the 12th century, with Indonesian, Arab and African contributions 'still actively discussed'; the 'Vazimba' were probably no single people but earlier highland inhabitants (Hebert: joking relations), Merina oral tradition (Tantara, collected 1868-83) has the Merina arriving between the 13th and 15th centuries on a slow penetration from the Bay of Antongil, not a massive invasion; kingdoms appeared after the 12th century, with Hindu-Indonesian elements (Ottino) and Arab-Muslim ones (Lombard, Raminia in the south-east; Antemoro sorabe in Arabic script), both disputed; Domenichini argues the royal sampy pre-date Muslim influence; Muslim influence strong in the 12th-14th centuries, Comoros as staging posts. Fills the Madagascar gap: say 'Indonesian-African-Arab, contested mix' and give no single origin story [CONTESTED]. Module 6.

column4: ch-025 chunk 2 (Madagascar trading posts, institutions)
column5: North-west Madagascar had Swahili-style trading posts (Mahilaka, Nosy Langany, Sada) exporting rice and soapstone and importing Indian pearls, cloth and Chinese ceramics, forming the Antalaotse city-states; the GHA (Esoavelomandroso, citing Chittick) says the coastal cities of East Africa 'were founded by Africans and not by Arabs'; Raminia/Antemoro Arab-ancestry stories are called status claims 'to attach themselves to the most celebrated sources of Islam'. Material culture: paddy rice Indonesian, zebu and yams African; first Malagasy kingdoms from the 15th century (south-east first); religion a blend (Zanahary from Indonesia, double funerals, sorcerers); archaeology 'only just beginning', radiocarbon dates needed. Module 6/Madagascar short note: Indonesian, African and Arab-Swahili mix, kingdoms from the 15th century, many dates uncertain [THIN EVIDENCE].

column4: ch-021 chunk 1 (Ogot, Great Lakes: sources and Kitara)
column5: Ogot (GHA IV, 1984): 1200-1500 in the interlacustrine region has scant oral, linguistic or archaeological data; Chwezi traditions are legendary (Wrigley says they contain no valid early history, 'like believing Odin and Freya were kings'), while Ogot, Oliver and Posnansky accept the Bachwezi as historical (Posnansky ties them to Bigo, dated 1350-1500) and Wrigley alone holds out [CONTESTED]; chronology has no agreed framework (Henige questions the Bito genealogy; Kagame's Rwanda genealogy from 959 vs Vansina's founding in the late 15th century, with Kagame's first seven names mostly non-historical); histories are court-centred and biased toward pastoralists as 'civilising conquerors'; 'pastoralist' and 'agriculturalist' are occupations, not ethnic labels, and people changed between them. Kitara: Batembuzi period about 900-1300 shows Bantu agriculturalists and iron-workers (Basita) forming small chiefdoms; Ndahura about 1344-71 and Wamara about 1371-98 ruled a loose empire on salt, cattle and iron; Bachwezi are argued to be a local Bantu aristocracy, not Hima or Luo invaders (Ogot's own view). Module 6: the course's Ntusi/Bigo/Buganda lesson should flag these dates as reconstructed, not recorded.

column4: ch-021 chunk 2 (Ogot, Bachwezi end, Luo and Hima, western lakes)
column5: Ogot: the Bachwezi fell to Kagoro's coup after famine and cattle disease, replaced by the Luo-Babito states (Bunyoro-Kitara, Kitagwenda, Kiziba) and Bahinda states (Nkore, Karagwe and others); the idea of a Luo army marching into Kitara 'must be discarded' (small groups moved over generations; Rukidi's Babito about 1436-63); Luo dispersal dated glottochronologically about 870 +-200 (he admits many linguists no longer trust glottochronology) and Tekidi's Owiny I (1409-36); Bachwezi 'disappearance' was successor propaganda; in the west, Bantu clans (Basiita, Bazigaaba, Bagyesera, Barengye iron-workers) formed the earliest dynasties before pastoralist rulers, and origins of the Bahinda (Ruhinda) are disputed three ways (Bachwezi descent, Nilotic per de Heusch refuted by Karugire, Gisaka Bagyesera per Denoon); pastoralists did not all start as rulers. Module 6: dates are reconstructed from generation counts and tradition [TRADITIONAL DATE].

column4: ch-021 chunk 3 (Ogot, Rwanda and Kintu complex)
column5: Ogot on Rwanda: he rejects the Kagame/White Fathers 'Hamitic Tutsi' conquest story as court-centred and based on the outmoded Hamitic theory (Tutsi bringing iron, kingship and caste); seven major pre-Nyiginya clan states existed (Singa/Renge, Zigaba/Mubari, Gesera/Gisaka, others), Gisaka was as organised as young Rwanda; pastoralists grew sharply from about the 15th century but coexisted peacefully, the vassalage system developed after 1500; Nyiginya state formed by the end of the 15th century (Rennie's chronology: Ndahiro Ruyange 1424-51, Ndoba 1451-78, Samembe 1478-1505); Mubari lost its drum Sera in the late 16th century and its dynasty ended in 1765-92. Ruhinda's composite date about 1405-47, he took the Bachwezi herds into Karagwe (Nyakatura's version accepted). Kintu: unclear whether he lived; Kintu is the symbol of a lion-leopard clan complex arriving with lungfish and other 'banansagwa' (found-in-place) clans, Bantu groups moving from the Elgon-Lake Victoria area 1100-1400. Module 6: Rwanda and Buganda origins should not rest on the Hamitic story.

column4: ch-021 chunk 4 (Ogot, Buganda and the Kimera complex)
column5: Ogot: Buganda grew from small Bantu agricultural states (Bugulu, Buddu's Bemba) before pastoralists mattered; Kintu is a symbol for a lion-leopard clan complex (unclear whether he lived) and Kimera (c. 1344-74 by this chapter's chronology) is 'the Kimera complex' of refugee clans of mixed origin fleeing the Bachwezi empire, so the 'Luo' or 'Hima' identity of Kimera depends on which clan's tradition is read (Crazzolara's bushbuck clan vs Kaggwa's grasshopper clan); Buganda tradition suppressed its Bachwezi links (Mukasa and Mugasha, Nyinamwiru and Namuddu parallels); thirty-five clans each presenting wives to the kabaka; migration and settlement period over by 1500. Module 6: Buganda's origin is reconstructed from clan traditions and the dates are generational [TRADITIONAL DATE].

column4: ch-017 chunk 1 (Kropacek, decline of Christian Nubia)
column5: Kropacek (GHA IV): the baqt treaty between Egypt and Nubia held about six centuries as the basis of peaceful relations, with Fatimid-era Nubia at its height; the political history is known almost entirely from Egyptian Arabic sources, local records of late Christian Nubia are scarce; two kingdoms Makuria (Dongola) and Alodia (Alwa), matrilineal succession; decline under Ayyubids and Mamluks: Baybars' 1276 expedition made Shakanda a vassal (half the revenue as tribute, jizya on non-converts), Mamluk campaigns 1276-1397, pressure of Arab nomads (Banu l-Kanz) moving south; Dongola's cathedral became a mosque on 29/05/1317 (tablet) under the Muslim king Abdallah Barshambu, the 'beginning of official conversion'; last written reference to a Nubian king 1397; Nubia 'was never annexed' and the kingdom 'turned inside out', with Arab fathers acquiring succession rights through Nubian mothers; archaeology (Aswan High Dam salvage) shows defensive walls, watchtowers and island settlements from about the mid-12th century. Source numbers (10,000 captives; 40,000 tribesmen 1289) are chronicle figures called exaggerated. Module 2: Christian Nubia ended gradually, not in one conquest [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-017 chunk 2 (Alwa, Funj, how Christianity ended)
column5: Alwa (Alodia): 400 churches and a cathedral at Soba per Abu Salih (early 13th century) but sparse sources afterwards; Soba's fall traditionally 1504 (Funj sultanate at Sennar) but Kropacek says the two events need not coincide, with an Arab chief Abdallah Jamma (Abdallabi) possibly taking Soba earlier; Funj origins disputed (Shilluk, Bornu, Ethiopia), the Funj and Abdallabi shared rule. Christianity persisted: a bishop buried at Qasr Ibrim with Coptic and Arabic scrolls was in office in 1372; Alvares in the 1520s heard of about 150 churches in Nubia whose people were neither Christian, Muslim nor Jewish; Adams: Nubian Christianity was destroyed 'more by accident than by design'; but the church was elite, urban and tied to Coptic clergy with few indigenous saints; Islamisation by traders, Arab immigration and royal conversion, gradual and not north-to-south uniform; Arab 'nisba' genealogies are suspect (the Funj claim Umayyad ancestry, the Jaaliyyin Abbasid); the Jaaliyyin are 'Arabized Nubians with only a small proportion of Arab blood'. Module 2: do not teach a single conquest or forced conversion; give the 1372 bishop as the last firm date of a bishop [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-017 chunk 3 (Nubia's society after the kingdom; links westward)
column5: Kropacek: the 'dark period' brought impoverishment, a lower Nile, shift from matrilineal to patrilineal organisation, Arabic language except in Nubian-speaking stretches, end of church art, and some Nubians turned semi-nomadic (Adams's hypothesis about Mahas and Kenzi dialects 'not unanimously accepted'); he warns that general nomadisation is an over-simplification; Red Sea trade via Aydhab (then Suakin) was Arab-run, Suakin paid Baybars 80 slaves, 300 camels and 30 qintars of ivory; Nubia-Ethiopia links are barely documented; claims that Nubia spread Christianity or culture to West Africa have 'some reservations' (Shinnie: eastern-origin traditions may reflect medieval Nubia rather than Meroe), red-brick sites in Kordofan, Darfur and Chad (Ayn Farah, Koro Toro) show possible links but are undated or unexcavated. Module 2: say Nubian influence westward is plausible but unproven [THIN EVIDENCE].

column4: ch-017 chunk 4 (Darfur, Bornu and the pilgrim road)
column5: Kropacek: Arkell's hypotheses on Darfur (Tundjur under Nubian protection; Dunama of Kanem about 1240) are speculative; institutions between the Nile and Chad show Bornu cultural influence, not necessarily political rule; a 1391 letter from Bornu's king to Sultan Barquq complains of Arab Judham raiders selling his people to slave dealers; the Sudan-road pilgrimage across Africa came only after the 16th century (earlier pilgrims such as Mali's and Songhai's rulers went by North Africa and Egypt). Module 2/8 side note.

column4: ch-011 chunk 1 (Lange, Kanem and the Sefuwa)
column5: Lange (GHA IV): Kanem is the only political entity of international renown between Nubia and the Niger Bend and has an internal source, the Diwan of the Sefuwa sultans (written from the first half of the 13th century, only about 50 pages, brought up to date until the 19th century); the Sefuwa replaced the Zaghawa-ruled Duguwa dynasty in the second half of the 11th century under Hummay (c. 1075-1180), probably of Berber origin whose Yemeni (Sayf b. Dhi Yazan) descent claim is a prestige genealogy; the chroniclers say what mattered was religion not colour (Salmama c. 1182-1210 'very dark', unlike earlier kings of 'the redness of Bedouin Arabs'); the capital moved from Manan to Djimi (further south), queen-mothers' origins (Tubu, Kay, Dabir, Magomi) show a growing weight for sedentary peoples; the Magomi are the Sefuwa patrilineage and nucleus of the Kanuri, so the state is older than the Kanuri people; the origin of the state is put at about the end of the 6th century. Module 4: Kanem-Borno's dates before 1200 come from the Diwan, a dynastic chronicle [TRADITIONAL DATE].

column4: ch-011 chunk 2 (Lange, Kanem's politics and trade)
column5: Lange: Kanem grew at the southern end of the Fezzan-Kawar caravan route; salt mines of Bilma and Fachi in Kawar were the richest in the central Sahara; the Diwan gives little on administration: from the 13th century the Sefuwa relied on non-royal officials (kagiama and yerima in Bornu times), queen-mothers (later the ghumsa) mattered, twelve vassal kingdoms by the end of the 15th century, standing army distinguished from levies; Kanem's prosperity rested more on farming, herding, salt-mining and crafts than on slaves, though slaves were a major export (al-Yaqubi 9th century; Leo Africanus: North African traders exchanged horses for slaves and waited a year); Dunama Dibalami (c. 1210-48) had 41,000 horses per the Diwan (a chronicle figure, [THIN EVIDENCE]); horses and cloth imported, cotton strips used as currency, a giraffe sent to Tunis in 1268; Kanem's control of the Fezzan in the 13th century is 'rash' to call an empire; the 'Mai Ali' tomb at Traghen is Idris b. Ali (c. 1677-96), not an earlier viceroy; the 1391 letter shows Muslim subjects being enslaved by Arab raiders. Module 4: Kanem-Borno was a trade-and-farming state, slaves not the sole base.

column4: ch-011 chunk 3 (Lange, Islam, Bornu, Bulala)
column5: Lange: Kanem's kings raided non-Muslim peoples south and around the lake, and the king's income depended on trans-Saharan trade and slaves obtained by raids, so it was not in their interest to spread Islam far; Islam did not take deep root even in Kanem before the 13th century; Dunama Dibalami (c. 1210-48) was the great Muslim reformer (destroyed the sacred mune, founded a madrasa in Cairo, per Ibn Furtuwa and al-Umari), though Hummay and Dunama b. Hummay are said to have made the pilgrimage; Kanem and Bornu were probably two kingdoms under one dynasty from the 13th century (Djadja/Kaka); Sefuwa left Kanem for Bornu at the end of the 14th century after the Bulala wars and Arab raids (Umar b. Idris c. 1382-87 killed by Judham Arabs), recaptured Djimi about 1497 under Idris Katakarmabi, and the Bulala were not decisively beaten until Idris Alawoma (1564-96); the Sao are a name for earlier peoples, 'no longer certain knowledge'; Leo Africanus's 'description' of the central Sudan is full of errors that rule out his having visited. Module 4. Dates from the Diwan [TRADITIONAL DATE].

column4: ch-011 chunk 4 (Lange, Sefuwa succession and the kayghamma)
column5: Lange reconstructs the Sefuwa rules of succession from the Diwan: father-to-son at first, collateral succession from the 13th century, a century-long Dawudid-Idrisid struggle (about 1366 to 1459) that ended with the Idrisids' victory, Bulala wars killing seven kings 1376-89, and for at least twenty years (c. 1421-40s) the kayghamma (army chief) and yerima made and unmade kings, 'the real masters of Bornu'; Ali Ghadjideni (c. 1465-97) built Gazargamo, the Sefuwa capital for over three centuries; Idris Katakarmabe (1497-1515) and Muhammad (1515-38) returned to father-to-son. All dates from the Diwan. Module 4 detail on Kanem-Borno politics; the dynastic dates are traditional.

column4: ch-010 chunk 1 (Izard, the Mossi of the chronicles)
column5: Izard (GHA IV): the Mossi who raid Gao (mid-13th century), take Timbuktu (about 1337 by Monteil's dating), take Walata (1480) and fight Sunni Ali (1464-92) and the askiyas (campaigns 1497-8, 1549, 1561-2, about 1575) are a strong military society somewhere in the Niger Bend, whose 300-year power ended in the 1561-2 campaign; he says the classical identification (Delafosse, Tauxier) of these 'Mossi of the Niger Bend' with the Mossi of the White Volta kingdoms (Mamprusi, Dagomba, Mossi) is only an unverified hypothesis built on similar names, 'never verified' and absent from Mossi oral tradition; the Say chronicle used by Boubou Hama is unpublished; the Mali king's 'relentless enemy' in al-Umari and Malfante's 1447 'king with 500,000 men' are possibly these Mossi, so numbers are legend-sized. Module 4: say the Songhai-Mossi wars are known only from the Timbuktu chronicles and the Mossi of the Volta kingdoms may be a different group [CONTESTED].

column4: ch-010 chunk 2 (Izard, Mossi origins and dates)
column5: Izard (GHA IV): Fage (1964) and Levtzion (1965/68) argue the Volta states are younger than the classical thesis said: Fage dates Na Nyaghse, founder of Dagomba, to about 1480, and Levtzion places the Mamprusi founding generation in 1380-1420; Izard's own genealogical method dates Yatenga to about 1540 and Naaba Wubri's Wagadugu to about 1495, with earlier reigns given only as an open table (generations of 15 to 30 years). Delafosse put the beginnings around the end of the tenth century, which Izard calls hazardous and unverified. Ancestors of the Mamprusi came from the east (Tohajiye the red hunter, Gurma, Kpogonumbo, Na Bawa); Mossi and Dagomba kings are linked through Yenenga by a uterine, not agnatic, line. Fifteen versions of the Mossi origin legend are known. Module 4/5: say Mossi, Mamprusi and Dagomba state dates are oral-genealogy reconstructions from the late 14th to 16th century [TRADITIONAL DATE][THIN EVIDENCE].

column4: ch-010 chunk 3 (Izard, Mossi kingdoms 15th-16th century)
column5: Izard (GHA IV): Mossi state history runs in three phases: preparation (second half of the 15th century, small southern commands around Zambarga and Kinzem), conquest (first half of the 16th century) and stabilisation (second half of the 16th century). Naaba Rawa, certainly historical, built the only Mossi 'empire' (Rawatenga), which fell apart quickly; Naaba Wubri founded Wagadugu (his date of 1495 is a formal hypothesis); Naaba Yadega founded Yatenga about 1540 (also a hypothesis) and Yatenga broke from Wagadugu under Naaba Geda at the end of the 16th century. Mossi frontiers on the west stopped at Boromo on the Black Volta; the Gurma formed a barrier to the east. Mossi system: 'people of the land' (tengsobondo, earth cult) versus 'people of power' (naam); institutions are known only from the late 18th century (Yatenga) and early 19th (Wagadugu), so the course must not project them back. Module 4 or 5: Mossi states as 16th-century creations from oral genealogies, not medieval empires [TRADITIONAL DATE].

column4: ch-010 chunk 4 (Izard, Volta peoples without states, economy)
column5: Izard (GHA IV): Mossi society split 'people of the land' (Gurunsi, Kurumba/Fulse, Dogon, Samo, Bisa, with earth cults) from 'people of power'; Yatenga succession by electoral college with no automatic rule, producing dynastic crises; institutions known only from the late 18th/early 19th century. Non-state Volta societies (Gurunsi, Bobo, Lobi, Dagari, Birifo) are known only from the 18th/19th century, with the south-west peoples crossing the Black Volta from the 16th. The economy for 12th-16th centuries is 'hypothetical extrapolation' from 19th-century travellers: millet, fonio, cotton, weaving and dyeing, Yatenga donkeys and Dongolawi horses, iron, Yarse long-distance trade (Saharan salt and fish north, kola south, cowries, cloth strips). Module 4: Volta basin is a trade link between Niger Bend and forest, but its early economy is extrapolated, not documented [THIN EVIDENCE].

column4: ch-002 chunk 1 (Niane, Introduction)
column5: Niane (GHA IV introduction): states Almoravids warred on Ghana 1050-1080 and Ghana 'finally collapsed in 1076', but also that the fall passed almost unnoticed and gold trade went on or grew; Abu Bakr died in Tagant 1087; Sundiata beat Sumanguru at Kirina in 1235, institutions 1230-1255; Mali's rulers converted 1050; caravans of 6000 or even 12 000 camels; slave export to the Arab world was exaggerated by some authors but no comparison with the Atlantic trade; states such as Kongo, Zimbabwe and Monomotapa owed little to Islam; Islam spread slowly and peacefully in the Sudan, courts not masses. Module 4: this editor's 1076 date is the same one volume III's Almoravid chapter doubts, so teach as a disagreement within the series [CONTESTED].

column4: ch-002 chunk 2 (Niane, Introduction, Zimbabwe and terms)
column5: Niane (GHA IV introduction): Zimbabwe and Mwene Mutapa reached their height between the 11th and 14th centuries (older than Fagan's chapter and current dating), 'Mwene Mutapa' read as 'lord of metals' by some and 'master pillager' by others (his note 4), Davidson's 'perhaps 60 000 or 70 000' ancient mines quoted, MacIver 1905 and Caton-Thompson 1931 cited for African origin, Portuguese da Goes and de Barros on 'Symbaoe'. The editor bans 'segmented', 'stateless', 'tribe', 'Hamitic' and 'fetishist' as terms, criticising the Hamitic hypothesis as colonial myth with a Rwanda/Burundi consequence; he gives Ibn Battuta's cowrie rate at Mali and Gao as 1150 to the gold dinar. Module 7: the 11th-14th-century span is the editor's, not Fagan's; module 1/4: terminology note. Also note Izard and Ngcongco-era chapters still use 'non-state' for Volta societies, so the series is not uniform [CONTESTED].

column4: ch-003 chunk 1 (Saidi, Almohads: religious background and Ibn Tumart)
column5: Saidi (GHA IV Ch 2): the Almohad period runs mid-12th to mid-13th century and aimed at unifying the Maghrib and Muslim West, with economic motives too: control of the northern outlets of the trans-Saharan routes and joining Maghrib growth points. Background: Maliki jurists' formalism dominant, Kharijite dissent among Berbers, Berber customary law lasting until Yusuf ibn Tashfin; al-Ghazali's attack on the jurists. Ibn Tumart: born about 1075 in the Anti-Atlas (Igiliz), of the Hargha, Masmuda group (Shluh); his Arabic name and Sharifian genealogy were invented; set out East in 1107; the claim that he met al-Ghazali is later hagiography, Ibn al-Athir denies it; met 'Abd al-Mu'min at Mallala; debated at Marrakesh before the Almoravid amir 'Ali ibn Yusuf; retreated to Aghmat, then Tinmallal (1123). Doctrine: tawhid, hence 'Muwahhidun' (Almohads); accused Almoravids of anthropomorphism and declared jihad on them; preached in Berber and used a council of notables. Module 3: supplies the Almohad end of the Almoravid story [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-003 chunk 2 (Saidi, Mahdism and Almohad organisation)
column5: Saidi (GHA IV Ch 2): Ibn Tumart proclaimed himself Mahdi (1121 at Igiliz, by ten companions including 'Abd al-Mu'min) after copying the Prophet's pattern (cave, hijra to Tinmallal in 1123); hadiths he cited were probably apocryphal; he rejected strict adherence to madhhabs, preferred Medinan tradition. Organisation: council of ten (Ahl al-Jama'a), council of fifty, talaba propagandists (1500 sent to the Sus in 1121 per Ibn Abi Zar'), the mass (al-kaffa) in ten-man units under a naqib with fourteen ranks; purges sometimes massacres; Tinmallal's original inhabitants probably liquidated; Masmuda groups resisted federation. After defeat at al-Buhayra Ibn Tumart died and 'Abd al-Mu'min replaced councils by shaykhs; Ibn Malwiya revolt about 1133; Caliph al-Nasir weakened shaykhs before Las Navas de Tolosa; al-Ma'mun later suppressed the Mahdi creed. Module 3 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-003 chunk 3 (Saidi, conquest under 'Abd al-Mu'min)
column5: Saidi (GHA IV Ch 2): the Almoravids beat the Almohads at al-Buhayra in 1128 (some sources 1130); Ibn Tumart died 1130 and 'Abd al-Mu'min acceded 1133 and reigned to 1163; he avoided the plains where Almoravid cavalry won and took the mountains first, partly for trade routes and mines (Sus, Draa essential to the Almoravids' sub-Saharan trade); Almoravid decline 1143 succession quarrel Lamtuna-Masufa, 1145 death of the Catalan Reverter; took Tlemcen, Marrakesh needed fifteen years to subdue Morocco; the Almoravid era was seen by chroniclers as peaceful and prosperous, so Almohads were not liberators outside the Masmuda; central Maghrib taken 1152 (Algiers, Bijaya, Qal'a sacked), Hilali Arabs beaten at Setif in 1153; Ait Amghar (Ibn Tumart's family) disgraced and 'Abd al-Mu'min made his son Muhammad heir in 1156-7, establishing the Mu'minid dynasty. Module 3 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-003 chunk 4 (Saidi, empire, Ifriqiya, tax, succession)
column5: Saidi (GHA IV Ch 2): Ifriqiya conquered 1159-60 (Tunis, Mahdiyya from the Normans after seven months, Gabes, Gafsa, Sfax, Tripoli), uniting the Maghrib for the first time; 'Abd al-Mu'min died 1163 at Sale before invading Spain; his policy had economic aims: he cut the Atlantic coast of Morocco, which the Almoravids had linked to the Sahara, from African contacts and secured the axis from the Draa to Oran as the caravan route for gold and goods from the western Sudan. He ordered a land survey from Barqa to Nul (a third deducted for mountains), the first land register since Roman times, charging kharaj on all but Almohad lands; the army was never unified; his Hilali transfer is judged by Saidi against Le Tourneau's colonial-era 'calamity'. Abu Ya'qub Yusuf (1163-84) took the caliph title in 1168, failed at Huete 1172-3; al-Mansur (1184-) faced the Banu Ghaniya (Almoravid heirs in the Balearics) who took Bijaya on 12 November 1184 (Huici Miranda gives 22 May 1185). Module 3: a trans-Saharan route shifted east of the Atlantic coast under the Almohads [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-003 chunk 5 (Saidi, Banu Ghaniya and Alarcos)
column5: Saidi (GHA IV Ch 2): the Banu Ghaniya (Almoravid heirs from the Balearics) fought the Almohads for about half a century: took Bijaya 1184, were beaten at Hamma 1187, Yahya rebuilt the coalition, took most of the eastern Maghrib by 1199-1200; al-Mansur won Alarcos on 18 July 1195 against Castile; al-Nasir took Majorca December 1203 (a naval and commercial base linked to Aragon, Genoa and Pisa), took Mahdiyya January 1206 and made the Hintata shaykh 'Abd al-Wahid viceroy of Ifriqiya (the origin of the Hafsids), Ibn Ghaniya captured only in 1233. Saidi argues the Banu Ghaniya struggle had a trans-Saharan economic dimension: their zone (Waddan, southeast Tripolitania to the southern Algerian oases) was the outlet of the great Saharan routes, so they were contending for the Fatimid, Zirid and Almoravid trade heritage; he rejects the colonial-era Marcais theory of the Hilali 'catastrophe'; Ibn Khaldun's 'not one fire still burns' is a later literary phrase. Module 3 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-003 chunk 6 (Saidi, Las Navas and break-up)
column5: Saidi (GHA IV Ch 2): Las Navas de Tolosa on 16 July 1212 was a symbolic defeat that Huici Miranda showed did not collapse Muslim Spain, with al-Nasir's purge of officers and Christian crusade (Rodrigo Jimenez de Rada, Innocent III) behind it; al-Nasir died 1213; the Almohad agony lasted over half a century: Banu Marin first appear near Fez 1218, al-Ma'mun (1227-32) renounced Mahdism in 1230 and relied on Christian militia, which began Christian trade privileges in Morocco, Hafsids under Abu Zakariyya broke away in Ifriqiya in 1228 and captured Ibn Ghaniya 1233, Spain lost from 1230 (Cordova 1236, Valencia 1238), Marinids took Marrakesh in 1269, a remnant Almohad power at Tinmallal until 1275. Saidi's gloss: Almohads lacked the commercial depth of the Sudan gold that Almoravids had, their axis ran east-west along the Tell (a 'guess' he flags). Module 3 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on Saidi's trade guess].

column4: ch-013 chunk 1 (Person, Upper Guinea coast peoples)
column5: Person (GHA IV Ch 12): Upper Guinea coast (Gambia to Bandama) was a 'second front' opened by the Portuguese in the 15th century; before that trade was by kinship relays and Malinke traders, kola exported to North Africa by the 12th century, malaguetta pepper reached Europe by the Sudan and Maghrib in the 14th-15th centuries. Coastal peoples (Balante, Felupe, Baga, Nalu, Landuma, Temne, Bulom, Kru) were rice-growing, fishing, autonomous lineage communities with no extensive kingdoms; Portuguese 'kings' were patriarchs or clan chiefs with councils that could overrule them (Valentim Fernandes); Bijago naval raiders with boats carrying 90-120; no Islam south of the Rio Grande; nomoli soapstone figures link to burial places; Sapes 'empire' was no state, a culture spreading by slow diffusion, not mass migration. Mali: tradition credits Tiramaghan Traore with Kaabu (Gabu), which lasted until 1867; Mali's sway did not go beyond Kurusa-Kankan-Odienne; Juula traders reached Begho and the Gulf of Guinea before the Portuguese; Soso invasion of Sierra Leone coast 1540-50. Person's volume author died December 1982. Module 5 (and 4) [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE: oral and retrospective].

column4: ch-013 chunk 2 (Person, Kaabu, Fulani, Mane, Cape Verde)
column5: Person (GHA IV Ch 12): Portuguese reached the Gambia in 1446 and the Rio Grande by 1456; Kaabu stayed loyal to a reduced Mali, contrary to old belief, and Bambugu gold stayed under Mali until 1599 (Mansa Mamudu beaten at Jenne), after which Kaabu was cut off and Mali dismembered about 1600-25; Fulani under Tengella arrived about 1450 and founded the Denianke dynasty of Futa Toro in the early 16th century, jihad of Karamoxo Alfa 1727; Mane invasion of Sierra Leone/Liberia 1540-50 (Mane-Sumba, Kwoja-Karu) was a small, snowballing elite that spread Mandingo language and centralised institutions but left the ethnic map largely unchanged, comparable to the Jaga and Zulu; the Vai and Kono came earlier (1460s or before); Malinke genealogies cannot reach back more than about four centuries so dates by generations are minimums. Cape Verde settled 1462; by 1582 Fogo and Santiago held 13,700 slaves, 400 free blacks and 1,600 whites; about 3000 slaves a year exported from the second half of the 16th century (his estimate). Lancados/tangomaos were Portuguese going native. Module 5/8 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on Mane dating].

column4: ch-014 chunk 1 (Kipre, Ivory Coast lagoons to the Volta)
column5: Kipre (GHA IV Ch 13): written sources only from Portuguese 1471-80 exploration; El Mina fort begun 1481 (gold the motive); Pacheco Pereira Esmeraldo 1505-6; Begho excavations (Posnansky) show trade with Jenne, site inhabited about 1100, kola market and Mali gold link in the 14th century, Akan society structured for intermediary trade; Segui ditches (4-6 m deep) undated; Aby lagoon middens undated; oral traditions rarely go before the 17th century; Ano Asena case (Perrot): the Ndenye ancestor who 'brought agriculture' is really about 1690, a myth rearranged after a migration, so oral genealogies can be telescoped. Akan and lagoon peoples are Kwa speakers (Volta-Comoe), Boahen refutes Mesopotamia/Libya/Ghana-empire origins and places origin in Chad-Benue region by linguistics (Greenberg); Akan are 45% of Ghana and 33% of Ivory Coast today; fundamental Akan structures developed between 1000 and 1500 (Posnansky, Boahen). Module 5 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE].

column4: ch-014 chunk 2 (Kipre, Akan foundations)
column5: Kipre (GHA IV Ch 13): the lagoon peoples lived in kinship communities under patriarchs with religious more than temporal power, exchanging salt, fish, cloth, gold and copper with the interior; Akan culture traits: matrilineal succession, day-names, 42-day ritual calendar (origin controversial), two clans (eight matrilineal, twelve patrilineal); Posnansky treats the 17th century as a turning point and no 14th-15th century Bron objects have been found; coastal states Asebu, Fetu, Aguafo and Fanti were small but organised for gold in the late 15th century, Begho capital of a Bron kingdom; queen-and-king joint rule is read as a passage from kinship society to kingdom with kingdoms fully structured by the end of the 16th century (Diabate, Rattray); Mandingo moved beyond Begho to El Mina after 1500. Module 5 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE].

column4: ch-015 chunk 1 (Ryder, ecology, kinship societies, Yoruba origins)
column5: Ryder (GHA IV Ch 14): forest peoples expanded from within the forest, glottochronology 'largely discredited'; Yoruba dialect groups (central Ife-Ilesha-Ekiti and south-east Ondo-Owo-Ijebu oldest, north-west Oyo group younger) agree with the Ife creation myth, not Johnson's east-migration Oyo myth; Igbo expanded from the Owerri-Umuahia homeland with yam and oil palm into independent lineage settlements, no Igbo state; village forms, age grades and secret societies cut across lineages; Ijo dispersion in the delta no later than the end of the 12th century; Horton's model: the compact village can generate state organs by internal adaptation, so no outside influence (Ghana, Sudan) is needed, though borrowing of rulers and swords of state among forest states is attested; forest states rarely rule beyond 60 km from the capital; copper from Takedda reached Ife, Benin and Igbo-Ukwu by the 9th-10th century (almost certain); Ife claims: Ita Yemoo charcoal radiocarbon dates +960 to +1160, earlier than other urban Yoruba sites; Ife origin claims by other peoples (Popo, Ijo claims of Benin origin) are prestige claims, not literal history; Ife legend lists first-generation states (Owu, Ketu, Benin, Ha, Sabe, Popo, Oyo) but king lists differ: Ijebu 52 rulers, Ife 47, Ketu 49, Sabe 21. Module 5 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on Ife-origin claims].

column4: ch-015 chunk 2 (Ryder, Oyo, Ife, Benin)
column5: Ryder (GHA IV Ch 14, 1984): the typical Yoruba state was one town and villages (16-17 Ekiti kingdoms; Egba and Ijebu small-state federations); Oyo is the exception but its 'imperial' character came late, perhaps early 17th century, founding date early 15th century from king list is only suggested, capital abandoned under Nupe pressure in the second quarter of the 16th century, reoccupied about the end of that century, cavalry emphasised and Egungun borrowed from Nupe, so unlikely to be consequential before 1500. Ife: first phase from about the 11th century (scattered settlement, potsherd floors, glass beads, naturalistic terracotta); potsherd floors from about 1100 but later ones carry maize impressions so not before the 16th century; terracotta style found also at Owo (15th century) so not exclusively Ife kingship; the 25 Ife heads are brass and copper, probably made just before a 16th-century catastrophe (conquest by an alien dynasty the likeliest explanation), so modern Yoruba kingship derives from the later phase. Benin: kingdom perhaps from the 12th century; Oranyan from Ife about 1300 by tradition; Ewuare in the 15th century turned a limited monarchy into an autocracy (Ryder suspects an alien conquest behind the brother-killing story), built wall and rampart, three palace departments, council of ozama, palace and town chiefs, primogeniture with edaiken title, Igue festival, conquered Edo and Ibo west of the Niger and some Yoruba, direct rule within about 64 km, Itsekiri kingdom founded by Ewuare's grandson Iginua; archaeology confirms wall and palace in the 15th century but all pre-16th-century brass found is forged; cire-perdue casting became important only in the 16th century with imported European brass; the iyoba head cannot be earlier than the first decades of the 16th century (Esigie). Module 5: corrects early dates for Oyo and Benin bronzes [CONTESTED, superseded by later work on Ife/Benin brass chronology].

column4: ch-015 chunk 3 (Ryder, Ife and Igbo-Ukwu art, Nupe, conclusion)
column5: Ryder (GHA IV Ch 14): Ife heads were first seen by Frobenius in 1910 and many sculptures were taken to England after an English column sacked Ife at the end of the 19th century (as the volume says); Fagg's Abiri heads show naturalistic and abstract styles in one tomb; Ife art religious (Oni's tomb heads), Benin tradition says an Ife sculptor taught Benin casting; Igbo-Ukwu (Thurstan Shaw, found 1939, 800 bronze pieces, ritual kingship, priest-king Ezi Nzi) has cire-perdue casting dated by radiocarbon to the 9th century, at least two centuries before Ife and Benin, contradicting Ryder's own hypothesis about brass casting; he warns charcoal dates can be old, equatorial radiocarbon doubted (Ozanne), one Igbo-Ukwu date 1445 plus or minus 70 and another site 1495 plus or minus 95, and the chronology 'must be re-examined'; Nupe 'Tsoede bronzes': Tsoede is legendary with a 128-year life in tradition (Willett: period obviously mythic); Takedda was the nearest copper source; Shaw suggests the power centre moved from Ife to Old Oyo to control the north-south trade. At the end of the 15th century Oyo and Benin were the most important states plus well-structured independent cities (Ijebu, Ijo trading states). Module 5 [CONTESTED: Igbo-Ukwu dating is a stated puzzle; later work (Shaw 1970 dates) supports the 9th century but the chapter leaves it open].

column4: ch-020 chunk 1 (Ehret, East African interior 1100-1600)
column5: Ehret (GHA IV Ch 19): reconstructs East African interior by historical linguistics: in 1100 Bantu speakers were still few and restricted to wetter land (900-1000 mm rain), with root and tuber farming; interior plains had Nilotic and Southern Cushitic mixed farmers and pastoralists; proto-Seuta of 1100 already had Indonesian crops (Asian yam, taro, banana); Bantu communities coexisted with hunter-gatherers (Boni, Dahalo); age-grade systems of Miji-Kenda and Pokomo came from Southern Nilotic influence before 1600 rather than the Galla in the 17th century; Lake Nyasa corridor Bantu (Njombe, Nyakyusa, Songea, Lapwa) expanded 1100-1600 and Wakinga immigrants founded Nyakyusa princely lines in the 16th century; east Victoria Bantu absorbed Southern Nilotes and Cushites (circumcision, cyclical age-sets) and lacked chiefship, unlike Lacustrine Bantu; the Kintu period in Busoga and Buganda tradition read as a settlement of north-east Victoria people about the 14th century introducing intensive banana farming (Cohen); Luo intruded into the Kavirondo Gulf area only in the 16th century; Southern Cushitic East Rift peoples (millet, sorghum, eleusine) were once widespread from Kilimanjaro to Dodoma and were broken by Dadog and Ongamo Nilotic expansion by 1100. Module 6 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE: linguistic reconstruction].

column4: ch-020 chunk 2 (Ehret, highlands, Takama, Kalenjin)
column5: Ehret (GHA IV Ch 19): Takama expansion (Iramba, Nyaturu, Nyamwezi-Sukuma, Kimbu) across western Tanzania began about 1000 and by 1600 Nyamwezi-Sukuma stretched from Lake Victoria nearly to Ukimbu, by absorbing Southern Cushites; the highland banana agriculture (irrigation, manure, Indonesian banana) developed by Bantu absorbing Southern Cushites on Kilimanjaro, Mount Kenya and Pare early in the second millennium, enabling the Chagga to spread over five centuries and Shambaa to settle the Usambaras by 1500; Taita Hills and Thagicu (Kikuyu, Meru) expanded 1100-1500 by cutting forest; Akamba identity crystallised in 16th-century Ukambani from Sabaki immigrants and Thagicu; Southern Nilotic Kalenjin spread from about 1000 across the Uasingishu plateau, South Kalenjin settled as far as the West Ruvu borders by 1500, Dadog held the Loita, Ngorongoro and Serengeti until Maasai invaders broke them in the 17th century; Iraqw and Sonjo irrigators. Module 6 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE: linguistic].

column4: ch-020 chunk 3 (Ehret, Maasai, exchange, markets)
column5: Ehret (GHA IV Ch 19): proto-Maasai split into Samburu, Tiamus and Maasai; the Maasai began moving along the Rift in central Kenya from the 16th century and may have reached northern Tanzania by 1600; immigrants never moved into empty land so history is one of conflict and exchange; Bantu spread through agricultural adaptability (shift from root crops to bulrush millet and sorghum, or highland banana farming); formal markets appeared only around Mount Kenya and Kilimanjaro (hides, wooden vessels, gourds, grain for livestock; Gweno of North Pare as iron suppliers, 16th century) and elsewhere not until well after 1600 under external influence. Reconstruction rests on linguistics (market terms in proto-Thagicu and early Chagga). Module 6 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE].

column4: ch-024 chunk 1 (Ngcongco with Vansina, Southern Africa peoples)
column5: Ngcongco and Vansina (GHA IV Ch 23, 1984): southern African history is hampered by apartheid-era historiography that rejected oral and archaeological sources and neglected Portuguese archives; Early Iron Age to about 1100 (Lydenburg heads 5th century; iron between Zambezi and Limpopo about 20 plus or minus 80 BC per Inskeep); Middle Iron Age 1100-1600 with new ways of life, Khoikhoi becoming pastoralists, cattle growing in importance; Bantu arrival was infiltration of small groups not a sweeping invasion; Ehret's lexico-statistics: Shona-Venda 55%, Tsonga-Shona 41%, Chopi 38%, Sotho 37%, Nguni 35%, so two centres (Shona in Zimbabwe, 'south-east Bantu' probably in northern Transvaal); Sotho/Tswana and Nguni split within South Africa, languages separated by about 1600; pottery is not a barometer of cultural change (Phalaborwa); Phalaborwa copper mining at least from the 8th century, earliest dated site 960-1130, Venda polity took over the Transvaal chiefdoms perhaps in the 17th century (Scully hypothesis that state arose from metalworking trade); villages of 10-20 huts around cattle kraal 1060-1610 near Rustenburg; stone-walled Type N sites at least as early as 1400-1450 in the Orange Free State, more widespread in the 17th century. Terms: 'Hottentot' derogatory (use Khoikhoi), 'San' a Khoikhoi word. Module 7 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE].

column4: ch-024 chunk 2 (Ngcongco with Vansina, Botswana, Nguni, Khoikhoi)
column5: Ngcongco and Vansina (GHA IV Ch 23): Denbow's 150+ Botswana sites 800-1300 show intensive cattle herding (manure deposits up to 1 m), with a population decline after about 1300 (drier climate or tsetse shift, or Zimbabwe centralising trade) possibly feeding Sotho-Tswana expansion into the Vaal region with lobola and cattle clientship (their hypothesis, flagged tentative); stone settlements built by ruling groups spread as prestige architecture; south of the Drakensberg only three Later Iron Age sites (Blackburn near Durban, Moor Park near Estcourt 13th-14th century, Umngazi in the Transkei undated); Xhosa ruling families on the upper Mzimvubu by the 16th century, Wilson's 1300 date 'an order of magnitude', 1686 Togu date uncertain; Nguni occupied nearly their 1800 territory by 1500; Khoikhoi influence 14% of Zulu and 20% of Xhosa vocabulary, milking, riding and pack oxen learned from them, Xhosa derive about 60% of genes from Khoisan stock; Khoikhoi belong to Tshu-Khwe language group, spread rapidly from Botswana after about 1300, were at the Cape by 1488 (Dias), killed Almeida and sixty Portuguese at Table Bay in 1510; Middledrift 11th century cattle site not Khoikhoi; Khoikhoi are of southern African hunter stock, not from elsewhere. Module 7 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED: Botswana-to-Vaal movement is hypothesis].

column4: ch-024 chunk 3 (Ngcongco with Vansina, Khoikhoi society, conclusion)
column5: Ngcongco and Vansina (GHA IV Ch 23): Khoikhoi expansion probably caused by climate deterioration at the Kalahari edge or a tsetse-belt shift, with Botswana abandoned by 1300; Khoikhoi politics were clans with hereditary chiefs and tribute links, based on individual cattle wealth so fortunes reversed within a generation, poor became strandlopers or hunters; Khoikhoi overran farming settlements east of the Kei and held the Transkei before farming density grew over a century or two and Xhosa dominance emerged in the 16th century; Herero borrowed Khoikhoi pastoralism and moved to Namibia from western Botswana, Vedder tentatively gives about 1550; hunters lost stock and became clients, 'San' meaning 'robbers' in Khoikhoi; no group is a 'pristine' hunter; origin of Botswana pastoralism 800-1300 is unaccounted (cattle terms not eastern Bantu; possibly Tshu-Khwe, Ehret's Central Sudanic idea thought slender). Module 7 [CONTESTED][THIN EVIDENCE].

column4: ch-026 chunk 1 (Niane, Sahara trade, salt, copper, slaves)
column5: Niane (GHA IV Ch 25): 1100-1500 is the 'golden age' of trans-Saharan trade, the Sahara 'never a barrier' and compared to a sea; Ibn Battuta's route: Sijilmasa, 25 days to Taghaza, ten days rest, Walata after two months, 51 days at Walata, 24 days to Niani; messenger paid 100 mithqal; Monod found buried cowries, copper bars and cloth in Mauritania (radiocarbon 1165 plus or minus 110); the mansa and Ghana's king monopolised gold nuggets and Mansa Musa hid gold sources; gold also from forest regions (Ivory Coast, Ghana, Nigeria) as well as Galam, Bure, Bambuk, but no export estimate is safe; salt: Walata 8-10 mithqal, Niani 20-30 or 40 mithqal (Ibn Battuta), salt and kola as small change; Takedda copper (Tigida) sold at about its weight in gold on 100 mithqal two-thirds gold (al-Umari), mithqal 4.25 g, thick bars 400 per mithqal; Ibn Battuta left Takedda with a caravan of about 600 women slaves; Mauny's tentative estimate 20 000 slaves a year or 2 million per century to the north (Niane thinks the slave trade to Arabs was no haemorrhage); Nubia's baqt: 442 slaves a year to Cairo (365 treasury, 40, 20, 5, 12); al-Makkari brothers of Tlemcen ran a family trading network across Sijilmasa and the Sudan; Jews in Tuat from the 8th-9th century, Fernandes on Walata. Module 3 and 8 [PROBABLE]; Mauny's number [THIN EVIDENCE].

column4: ch-026 chunk 2 (Niane, Islam, Chad routes, forest filter, salt)
column5: Niane (GHA IV Ch 25): Italian traders in the Sudan (Benedetto Dei claimed Timbuktu 1469-70; Malfante's letter from Tuat), caravans 12 000 camels per Ibn Khaldun but average 1000 on normal Niger-Maghrib routes; Islamisation peaceful via Berber-Arab traders, Wangara and Hausa, matrilineal succession in Ghana (uncle to nephew) not caused by Arab influence; Ibn Battuta saw Kharijite whites among the Diafunu; Mansa Musa brought writers and an architect (audience hall received Ibn Battuta in 1353 under Sulayman); Bambara 'those who reject the mansa' (footnote) said to have split from Malinke under Musa; Kanem-Bornu routes (Fezzan, Bilma-Tibesti, Ghat-Ghadames) most used in the 15th-16th century; Hausa middlemen, Zaria bridgehead to the forest; Shaw: copper trade savannah-forest may go back to the 9th-10th centuries and Igbo-Ukwu copper came from Takedda; the forest as a 'filter', not a barrier; Dioula/Wangara = trader; Kong city traditionally dated to Sundiata but excavation has not confirmed; Begho linked with Jenne from the 12th century; kola circuits (Guro screen); salt in East Africa: Uvinza pans from the 5th-6th century, Ivuna 13th-15th century, Bankalie salt exported from Aksum 3rd-4th century, Kongo salt a royal monopoly. Module 3/4/6 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE for oral traditions].

column4: ch-026 chunk 3 (Niane, copper and southern gold)
column5: Niane (GHA IV Ch 25): copper mining began in the first centuries AD in Shaba, the Zimbabwe plateau and the upper Limpopo, copper bars and crosses traded and possibly used as money, the Portuguese first called the Limpopo the 'copper river'; al-Mas'udi (10th century) knew Sofala gold; Summers: mining began about the 7th century south of the Zambezi (Mazoe), spread over the plateau in the 9th-11th centuries, reached the Limpopo area only in the 15th; his estimate of 9-10 tons per year in the 11th century 'to be treated with caution', yet Niane says several thousand tons of gold went north each year in the 13th-14th centuries, a figure with no source, impossible against known African production, so unusable [THIN EVIDENCE]; most historians say Zimbabwe's wealth came first from cattle (tsetse-free plateau, a 13th-century drought pushing graziers up), gold control a century or two later, Sabi trade concentration and navigation changes explaining decline (Randles); Zimbabwe Acropolis has gold-smelting evidence; Luba-Lunda in Shaba before 1500; Vansina on bells crossing the equatorial forest, found at Ife and in Zimbabwe after 1400; Verin: Madagascar chlorite-schist objects reached Kilwa; the volume's call for research. Module 7 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED]; Module 3/8 for the forest-as-filter point.
