column4: ch-027 chunk 1 (Devisse and Labib, Africa seen from outside)
column5: Devisse and Labib (GHA IV Ch 26): Wangara (Takrur/Mali merchants) knew the Muslim world's geography; Wangara not in Arab sources before the 11th-12th century, later replaced by Dioula; black ambassadors resident in Cairo late 15th century; Ibn Khaldun still relied on Ptolemy and al-Idrisi, said equatorial regions uninhabited yet admitted perplexity ('a civilization... but it cannot amount to much') and in a footnote called southern peoples 'nearer to animals', a racist theory the chapter quotes as scholastic; Dulcert's 1339 map shows 'Rex Melli'; Cresques maps put the key to the south at Tlemcen; Malfante 1447 Tuat probe; Egypt barred Christians south of Cairo and the Red Sea from the end of the 12th century; Prester John; Iberian Christians sought gold; Mediterranean states fought among themselves (Marinids, Granada, Hafsids, Genoa), the Sahel drew into world trade slowly from the 7th to 10th century then fast in the 11th-12th; states grew up at northern convergence points of southern routes (Fatimids, Umayyads of Spain, Almoravids, Almohads each controlled terminal points). Module 3/8 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-027 chunk 2 (Devisse and Labib, European merchants and gold)
column5: Devisse and Labib (GHA IV Ch 26): Mali and Songhay controlled exports and diversified routes and customers; Venice, Genoa, Catalonia traded differently (Genoese bulk trade, sugar, Atlantic islands, ties with Portuguese discovery); African gold supplied Fatimid, Umayyad, Almoravid, Almohad and Hafsid coinage; trade with Tunis brought Christians about 20 000-60 000 dinars a year, Bijaya 12 000-24 000; Genoa imported 68 000 pounds of gold in 1377 and about 45 000 ducats a year later; Aragon got about 70 kg a year and Heers says Genoa 200 kg; tribute and ship/troop hire (Tunis paid Sicily 33 000 bezants a year in the 12th century); Gold exports from west and south Africa to the north perhaps 4 to 8 tonnes a year, 'ridiculously small' against Europe's needs (this contradicts the several thousand tons in Niane's Chapter 25); customs duties about 10%, Tunis customs 150 000 dinars a year in the 15th century. Module 3/8 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE: 4-8 tonnes is 'perhaps'].

column4: ch-027 chunk 3 (Devisse and Labib, slaves to Europe, Red Sea and Indian Ocean)
column5: Devisse and Labib (GHA IV Ch 26): Mediterranean slave trade: black slaves in Sicily 12th-13th century, Catalan and Italian merchants shipped them in the 14th-15th century, Cyrenaica key 1440-70, 83% of Naples slaves black in the second half of the 15th century, 'Guinea' blacks first recorded in Barcelona 1489, Portugal's Cortes in 1472 demanded control of re-export, Lisbon received 3589 slaves from 15 June 1486 to 31 December 1493 (at least 1648 for Florentine merchants), Valencia sold about 800 slaves in 1495-6, prices collapsed; the authors say fifteenth-century Atlantic expansion 'brutally interrupted' the 14th-century growth. Indian Ocean: Karimi merchants (name possibly linked to Kanem, uncertain) ran spice, gold and copper trade via Aden and Egypt, Aydhab busy port under the Ayyubids (Ibn Jubayr 1183), Egypt's need for gold in the 12th century when Wadi al-Allaki was exhausted; East African exports iron (to India, al-Idrisi, Ibn al-Wardi about 1240), ivory, hides, gold; Sofala gold marketed at Kilwa, Summers puts output at 10 tonnes a year, declining from the 15th century; 67% of Kilwa customs from imported cotton in the 13th century; over fifty Swahili towns before Arab immigration and Shirazi myth a late formulation (15th century at earliest); Kilwa struck coins from the 13th century; African sailors on coasters. Module 6 (Swahili) and 8 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on gold magnitude].

column4: ch-027 chunk 4 (Devisse and Labib, China and the Atlantic)
column5: Devisse and Labib (GHA IV Ch 26): Cheng Ho (Zheng He) made seven voyages 1405-1433 and called at the African coast twice, 1417-1419 and 1431-1433, with the giraffe delegation from Malindi to Peking in 1415 (their date, awkward against 1417); Matveiev in Ch 18 gives 1417-19 and 1421-22 for the voyages that reached Africa, so the volume disagrees internally on the second East African call; Chinese porcelain at Songo Mnara from about 1127-1450; Chinese ships about 1500 tonnes vs first Portuguese Indian Ocean ships 300 tonnes; Covilha 1487, Diaz 24 July 1488, da Gama 1497-8 met Ibn Majid; the 'Atlantic Mediterranean' conquest was not technical but commercial (Italian capital, Genoese sugar, timber), Muslims had no economic reason to compete at sea; caravels two or three times smaller than Venetian ships; Madeira sugar 70 000 arrobas in 1508, Guanche slavery before African slavery; Portuguese reduced Africa to a supplier of manpower; al-Umari's account of the Mali predecessor's 200-ship Atlantic voyage (the Abu Bakr II story) quoted as source. Module 6 (Zheng He) and 8 [CONTESTED][PROBABLE].

column4: ch-027 chunk 5 (Devisse and Labib, Portuguese expansion, early slave trade, Mali Atlantic voyage)
column5: Devisse and Labib (GHA IV Ch 26): the al-Umari story of the mansa who sent 200 then 2000 ships west is taken seriously but with no consequences; Mauny says the voyage was technically impossible, the authors defuse the technical debate; Portugal rounded Bojador 1434, took nine years to master the return by the Azores, expansion from 1443; Portuguese gold from all Atlantic coasts never exceeded and perhaps never attained 1 tonne a year; Mauny estimates West-to-North Africa gold under 4 tons a year (so 4-8 tonnes earlier and under 4 later); trade disappointing (Felou rapids 1481, Zaire rapids 1483, Wadane 1487, Cantor controlled by Mali); malaguetta pepper replaced by Asian pepper; Prester John not found; Sao Tome occupied 1472 for sugar; slave trade rhythm from 1440 (Mauritanian coast, Zurara's justification), Lagos company 1444 (240 slaves shared), Arguin 'regular trade' from 1448 (several hundred a year), after 1460 about 1000 a year from Cape Verde to Sine-Saloum, Verlinden estimates about 880 a year arriving in Portugal, Pope Nicholas V bull of 8 January 1454, Marchionni's lease 45 000 ducats a year (1486-8), Curtin's estimate 175 000 slaves taken from Africa in the 15th century (plus Verlinden's numbers). Module 8 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE for totals]; Module 4 for Mali's Atlantic voyage as [CONTESTED].

column4: ch-027 chunk 6 (Devisse and Labib, horse rate and Senegambian society)
column5: Devisse and Labib (GHA IV Ch 26): slave-for-horse rate fell with time and settled at roughly six slaves per horse (Ca da Mosto: 14 in the north at first, 10-12 in Senegambia, 6-15 at Sine-Saloum late 15th century), whereas Ly-Tall in Chapter 7 gives one horse for eight slaves, soon one for fifteen: the volume's two chapters disagree on direction, so M8's reading of Ly-Tall plus Reader as 'rose in slaves over time' must be flagged; Europeans barely penetrated the interior in the 15th century; Mali embassy 1481-95 failed; Kongo king Nkuwu baptised 3 May 1491, apostasy 1493-4 over polygamy; Senegambia: Mali blockade on iron, Jolof Burba demanded horses from 1455, regularised 1484; before Europeans Senegambia had griots, weavers, blacksmiths and cobblers but no merchants, the king ran trade, slavery existed (wars, debts, famine) but society not based on it, and the need to 'deal in slaves' to pay for horses and iron changed relations quickly and brought royal profit and social disrepute. Module 8 [CONTESTED on horse rate][PROBABLE].

column4: ch-028 chunk 1 (Niane, Conclusion: religion, politics, Mapungubwe and metals)
column5: Niane (GHA IV Ch 27 Conclusion): 15th-16th centuries a turning point; Columbus's gold and silver soon surpassed Bure, Bambuk, Ngalam and Mwene Mutapa; Islam in the Sudan a thin veneer of courts and merchants, ancestral religion unchanged, similar court ceremony at Koumbi, Niani and Yatenga (prostration with dust); clans stayed as federations (Marinid, Hafsid, Sa'dian, Mali, Mossi, Rwanda, Mwene Mutapa); Nubia: Christianity an elite religion (Kropacek quoted); Vansina quoted: Sanga and Katoto necropolises before 1000 show old Luba-type states; 'Rhodesian Ancient Ruins Ltd' pillaged Zimbabwe-Mapungubwe tombs; Mapungubwe flourished 'at least between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries, if not earlier' (this is Niane's loose claim, not Fagan's); iron may have been worked in southern Africa before the Christian era; Zimbabwe is the work of the Shona; African rulers controlled gold, copper and iron, banned Arab travellers from gold areas, Mansa Musa paid architects and scholars in gold, Zimbabwe rulers paid gold for Chinese porcelain; cotton introduced into the Sudan by Arabs before the 10th century (his claim); book trade at Gao and Timbuktu. Module 7 [CONTESTED: Mapungubwe date range, iron before Christian era]; Module 4 and 2 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-028 chunk 2 (Niane, Conclusion: economy, slaves, population)
column5: Niane (GHA IV Ch 27 Conclusion): agriculture the basis of the economy even under the kaya maghan, mansa and Mwene Mutapa; land held by the community not private; 'human estates' worked by communities paying fixed rent (Cissoko), serfdom more than slavery, but in the central Sudan (Hausa cities) slaves were numerous, crown versus house slaves (Salifou); 'hordes of slaves' did not build the monuments; Mali had 400 towns (Mahmud Ka'ti), a single Songhai fanfa could supply over 1000 sounu of about 70 kg, Gao king's regular army of 100 000 (his claim), towns perhaps 10 per cent of the population; Africa not under-populated, but his estimate of 200 million for the whole continent in Ibn Battuta's lifetime 'at a minimum' is far above what other estimates support and has no stated basis [THIN EVIDENCE]; the Portuguese were driven off by Dutch, English and French around 1550 (loose); slave trade before 1600 limited; ancient trade; call for oral tradition collecting (Galaal Somali astronomy); brass casting widespread (Ife, Igbo-Ukwu, Nupe, Guinea-Bissau figurines). Module 4 and 8 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE on totals].
